newsitem.title: USA: Investors buy dollars as safe haven after Deng's death.
newsitem.headline: Investors buy dollars as safe haven after Deng's death.

text.p: The dollar rose against most major currencies Wednesday, hitting session highs on news that China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping had died.
Investors bought dollars, traditionally a safe-haven in times of political turmoil, as rumours began to swirl in the currency market that the ailing 93-year-old Deng had died.
The dollar spiked to a session high of 1.7005 German marks but quickly returned to its previous trading level before China's Xinhua news agency stamped the rumours official.
Xinhua reported that Deng died late Wednesday of complications from Parkinson's disease and a lung infection.
Meanwhile, the dollar steadily inched higher against the Japanese yen, closing near its session high of 124.48 yen.
"They were buying dollars and dollar/mark popped up past a resistance level at 1.70 marks, but it has come off since," said Doug Lee, an assistant vice president at Sakura Bank Ltd. in New York.
Dealers said the market had widely anticipated the news.
"So while it causes a bit of uncertainty at the moment, I can't imagine anyone is shocked or surprised by this," said John Williams, chief global markets economist at Bankers Trust Co.
"If you use the old theory of buy the rumour, sell the fact, the flip side is now that the bad news is out, onward and upward for the markets," he added.
The dollar rose to 124.43 yen late Wednesday from 123.86 yen late Tuesday, and to 1.6980 marks from 1.6855 marks. The U.S. currency also gained to 1.4856 Swiss francs from 1.4705.
Earlier, the dollar rose amid heavy buying by large, speculative money funds.

"All I'm hearing is that U.S. hedge funds are buying some dollars, both dollar/yen and dollar/mark," said Thomas Arnold, a vice president and chief dealer of foreign exchange at Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank in New York.
Some dealers expressed surprise over the dollar's sharp reversal of fortune on Wednesday, a day after its steep slide against most major currencies.

"I am a little surprised. People did liquidate yesterday, selling dollars and buying marks and yen, but it seems like everything has reversed," said Ben Strauss, an associate vice president at Bank Julius Baer & Co.
The dollar suffered a minor set back in early U.S. trade after the Commerce Department released surprisingly strong U.S. international trade data for December.
The overall U.S. trade gap widened 29.6 percent to $10.29 billion in December from a revised $7.94 billion in November.

Simultaneously, the dollar was also hit by a Labour Department report showing consumer prices remained well-behaved in January. The Consumer Price Index rose a tame 0.1 percent in January, less than the 0.3 percent increase expected by Wall Street economists.

Neither set of data was seen as supportive of the dollar, with soft inflation figures taking the pressure off the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates and the trade gap growing more than expected. But dealers said the figures were not shocking enough to erase positive dollar sentiment.
The U.S. currency remained largely unfazed by conflicting statements from Geman central bank officials overnight.

The Bundesbank's February monthly report and remarks from its chief, Hans Tietmeyer, weighed on the dollar in European trade. The report said the mark's rally since early 1995 had more than corrected. Also, the German mass-circulation Bild newspaper quoted Tietmeyer as saying he hoped the dollar's long-term rise against the mark was at an end.

However, a subsequent media report quoted Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke as saying a dollar worth 1.70 to 1.75 marks would not risk importing inflation into Germany and boosted the U.S. currency.
In other trading, sterling rose to $1.6153 from $1.6065 and the dollar rose to Canadian $1.3597 from C$1.3543.
